item.title: AWS Launches AWS-LC, a Standardized Cryptographic Library for PQC
item.description:
AWS Launches AWS-LC, a Standardized Cryptographic Library for PQC

AWS has released AWS‑LC, a unified cryptographic library that supports post‑quantum algorithms while maintaining compatibility, assurance, and performance.

🔍 Overview

  • AWS‑LC is a general‑purpose cryptographic library maintained by AWS.
  • Derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL.
  • It provides hybrid post‑quantum key exchange via s2n‑tls for service endpoints.
  • It underlies aws‑lc‑rs (Rust), rustls, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider (Java).
  • AWS‑LC keeps an OpenSSL‑compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without rewriting.
  • AWS uses it across its services; if you’ve called an AWS API, AWS‑LC was used on the server side.

🧩 How it Works

  • AWS‑LC uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct.
  • It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce latency and compute costs of new algorithms.
  • For TLS, AWS‑LC libssl keeps an OpenSSL‑compatible API; most applications that use OpenSSL for TLS build against it with small changes.
  • Applications that call libcrypto directly may need more work, as the API differs in places.
  • When new algorithms are added, s2n‑tls, s2n‑quic, aws‑lc‑rs, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider adopt them automatically.
  • Hybrid ML‑KEM key exchange is enabled through existing TLS configuration APIs.
  • 1Password used AWS‑LC to move clients to hybrid post‑quantum key exchange with only a one‑line Cargo.toml change and no application code changes.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Three properties that reduce cost and friction of cryptographic updates:
    • Compatibility: update doesn’t require application changes.
    • Assurance: new code can be trusted when it ships.
    • Performance: new algorithm doesn’t add much computational overhead or latency.
  • AWS‑LC long‑term support (LTS) releases keep a stable application binary interface (ABI).
  • Applications link once, then take library updates without a rebuild.
  • One update reaches every application on the host when each process restarts.

🚀 Availability

  • AWS‑LC is available as an AWS‑LC library for C/C++.
  • The Rust bindings are available via aws‑lc‑rs.
  • Java integration is available via Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Every cryptographic algorithm has an expiration date; traditional ones like MD5 and SHA‑1 have been retired.
  • Standards are revised and flaws found in implementations.
  • PQC is accelerating the pace of adding new algorithms and removing old ones to keep up with regulations and risk.
  • The move to PQC has government and regulator deadlines; PQC will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post‑quantum algorithms.
  • Each change reaches systems as a software library update; the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version and its cost.
  • By standardizing on a single library like AWS‑LC, organizations reduce ongoing responsibility and operational risk.

📊 Performance Impact

  • TLS1.3 setup time on Graviton4 is measured for different algorithms; the figure shows impact of new algorithms.

  • Client‑server architecture using hybrid ML‑KEM.

#Cryptography #PostQuantum #AWSLC #Security

Source: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Migrating AWS CloudHSM Workloads to AWS KMS
item.description:
Migrating AWS CloudHSM Workloads to AWS KMS

AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) now supports the security certifications, algorithms, and performance required by most AWS CloudHSM workloads, enabling organizations to migrate and significantly reduce costs while eliminating hardware security module (HSM) provisioning, patching, and high-availability management.

🔍 Overview

Most AWS CloudHSM workloads can migrate to AWS KMS. Organizations are advised to review their compliance documentation for explicit single-tenant language, as many organizations find that it is assumed rather than mandated. While AWS KMS embeds cryptographic best practices in a managed service, some payment systems still rely on older cryptography such as TDES. For these cases, AWS Payment Cryptography supports payment use cases, including TDES-based algorithms such as CVV2, ARQC, and PIN validation, and provides low-level algorithms like AES-CBC that third-party systems might require for interoperability.

🧩 How it works

Migration consists of three parts: updating application code to call KMS APIs, rotating or importing cryptographic keys, and transitioning existing data.

  • Application Refactoring: This is the bulk of the effort. The interfaces involved are a communication pattern, not an architectural constraint. Organizations are encouraged to contact their AWS account team to assess the effort needed to use modern RESTful interfaces and to evaluate whether dependencies on older systems can be retired as part of security modernization.
  • Key Management: If AWS CloudHSM allows you to export (wrap) a copy of your private key, you can import it directly into AWS KMS to maintain continuity. If the key is non-exportable, you must create a new key pair in AWS KMS. During the transition, the AWS CloudHSM private key continues to sign existing workloads, while a new asymmetric KMS key (or the imported key) signs new data flowing to AWS KMS.
  • Data Transition: You re-encrypt previously encrypted data under KMS keys. Existing signatures remain verifiable without AWS CloudHSM. You can complete each part of the migration gradually with zero downtime. For organizations that created a new key pair, export the CloudHSM public key before decommissioning and use it to verify existing signatures locally with libraries such as AWS-LC or OpenSSL.

⚙️ Key details

The following points outline specific considerations and capabilities for the migration:

  • AWS KMS does not support importing public keys.
  • Traffic can be shifted from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS at your own pace.
  • Per-operation pricing is only one of several factors affecting cost; organizations should also consider saved staff time, patching, and high-availability management.
  • With envelope encryption, optional data key caching can further reduce API call volume.
  • Because application code is being refactored, this migration provides an opportunity to adopt post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms when creating new signing keys.
  • AI-assisted code transformation tools can reduce the workload associated with application refactoring.

💡 Why it matters

Migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS allows organizations to eliminate the operational overhead of managing HSMs while retaining the security features required for their workloads. The process supports a gradual transition with zero downtime and opens the door to modernizing cryptographic dependencies, including the adoption of post-quantum algorithms.

#AWSKMS #AWSCloudHSM #SecurityMigration #Cryptography #PostQuantum

Source: Reduce operational overhead by migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Asqav Releases Python and TypeScript SDKs for AI Agent Evidence
item.description:
Asqav Releases Python and TypeScript SDKs for AI Agent Evidence

Asqav has released Python and TypeScript SDKs to provide verifiable evidence of AI agent actions through an evidence layer.

🔍 Overview

The SDKs enable AI agents to generate signed, hash-chained compliance receipts for every action. These receipts are timestamped against independent witnesses and can be verified by auditors, regulators, or counterparties without an Asqav account.

🧩 How it works

  • Cryptography: Server-side cryptography is used, meaning there are zero native dependencies in either SDK.
  • Algorithms: The algorithm used is per-receipt from signature.alg, utilizing ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, post-quantum) for cloud-issued receipts and Ed25519/ES256 for locally signed ones.
  • Verification:
    • Users with a signature_id can verify without an API key.
    • The verify() function returns a public verdict and recomputes the chain_hash locally as the SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 canonical payload.
    • Offline, zero-trust checks that reproduce the signature can be performed via asqav.verify_receipt_offline(receipt, jwks) in Python, verifyReceiptOffline() in TypeScript, or a standalone CLI command: python -m asqav.verifier.verify_receipt --offline.

⚙️ Key details

Component Details
Python SDK pip install asqav (Requires Python 3.10+); tested on 3.10, 3.11, 3.12
TypeScript SDK npm install @asqav/sdk (Requires Node 20.19-20.x or 22.12+); tested on Node 20, 22
Integrations Works with LangChain, CrewAI, and MCP
Diagnostics asqav doctor validates configuration and connectivity when ASQAV_API_KEY is set

🚀 Availability

Asqav offers three plans:

  • Free: No credit card required.
  • Pro: Paid monthly or annual subscription.
  • Enterprise: Custom and volume-priced.

This development is profiled in the IETF Internet-Draft draft-marques-asqav-compliance-receipts and the Independent Submission profiling draft-farley-acta-signed-receipts.

#AIagents #SDK #Cryptography #Compliance #PostQuantum
